subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Abdominal aorta, watershed areas, and compression syndromes
vignette: During an anatomy review, a student examines the branches of the abdominal aorta. She notes that the vessels supplying the gastrointestinal tract arise as single midline vessels whose branches point anteriorly, whereas vessels to non-GI organs arise as paired vessels directed laterally and posteriorly. She is asked to state the rule that distinguishes the celiac trunk, SMA, and IMA from the renal and gonadal arteries.
question: Which of the following best summarizes the branching pattern of the abdominal aorta?

options.text: Arteries supplying non-GI structures are single and branch anteriorly.
Arteries supplying GI structures are single and branch anteriorly.
Arteries supplying GI structures are paired and branch laterally and posteriorly.
All abdominal aortic branches are paired and directed posteriorly.
Arteries supplying non-GI structures are single but branch anteriorly.

explanation_correct: Arteries supplying GI structures (celiac trunk, SMA, IMA) are single and branch anteriorly to reach the gut tube. Arteries supplying non-GI structures, such as the renal and gonadal arteries, are paired and branch laterally and posteriorly. This pattern reflects the original anterior projection of the embryologic gut and is a classic anatomy-lab distinction.

explanation_incorrect.A: This reverses the rule: single, anteriorly branching vessels supply the GI tract, while non-GI vessels are paired and posterolateral.
explanation_incorrect.C: GI arteries are unpaired midline vessels; it is the non-GI arteries, such as those to the kidneys, that are paired and posterolateral.
explanation_incorrect.D: The abdominal aorta gives both unpaired anterior visceral branches and paired lateral or posterior branches; they are not all paired.
explanation_incorrect.E: A single anteriorly branching pattern characterizes GI arteries; non-GI arteries arise as paired lateral or posterior vessels.

educationalObjective: GI arteries are unpaired with anterior branches, whereas non-GI arteries are paired with lateral or posterior branches.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Abdominal aorta, watershed areas, and compression syndromes
vignette: A 68-year-old man with severe atherosclerosis develops profound hypotension after a myocardial infarction. He passes bright red blood per rectum, and colonoscopy shows ischemic changes at two locations known to have a dual (watershed) blood supply: the splenic flexure and the rectosigmoid junction.
question: Which of the following correctly identifies the arterial sources at these two watershed areas?

options.text: Splenic flexure: celiac trunk and SMA; rectosigmoid: IMA and superior rectal artery.
Splenic flexure: SMA and IMA; rectosigmoid: superior and inferior rectal arteries.
Splenic flexure: SMA and IMA; rectosigmoid: last sigmoid branch of the IMA and superior rectal artery.
Splenic flexure: celiac trunk and IMA; rectosigmoid: middle and inferior rectal arteries.
Splenic flexure: left and right colic arteries alone; rectosigmoid: IMA and internal iliac artery.

explanation_correct: The splenic flexure lies at the junction of the SMA and IMA territories. The rectosigmoid junction is supplied by the most distal sigmoid branch of the IMA and the superior rectal artery, the terminal IMA branch. Because both areas depend on the most distal arterial branches, they are susceptible to colonic ischemia in hypotensive states and with thromboemboli or atheroemboli.

explanation_incorrect.A: The celiac trunk does not reach the splenic flexure; that watershed is between SMA and IMA territories, even though the rectosigmoid pairing listed here is correct.
explanation_incorrect.B: The rectosigmoid watershed involves two IMA-related vessels; the inferior rectal arteries arise from the internal iliac (systemic) circulation instead.
explanation_incorrect.D: Neither pairing is correct: the splenic flexure is an SMA/IMA border zone, and middle and inferior rectal veins and arteries belong to the systemic internal iliac system.
explanation_incorrect.E: Left and right colic arteries are both SMA branches, so together they do not create a dual supply; the internal iliac artery does not supply the rectosigmoid watershed.

educationalObjective: The splenic flexure (SMA/IMA) and rectosigmoid junction (last sigmoid branch of the IMA/superior rectal artery) are the colon's ischemic watershed areas.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Abdominal aorta, watershed areas, and compression syndromes
vignette: A 21-year-old thin man reports left flank pain and two episodes of gross hematuria. Physical examination reveals a left-sided varicocele. CT demonstrates a dilated left renal vein with narrowing as it passes between two major abdominal vessels just distal to its origin from the vena cava.
question: Compression of which vessel by which structures best explains these findings?

options.text: Left renal vein compressed between the SMA and abdominal aorta.
Left renal vein compressed between the IMA and abdominal aorta.
Third portion of the duodenum compressed between the SMA and aorta.
Right renal vein compressed between the SMA and IVC.
Left renal artery compressed between the abdominal aorta and SMA.

explanation_correct: Nutcracker syndrome is compression of the left renal vein between the SMA and the abdominal aorta. Impaired venous drainage raises left renal venous pressure, causing flank pain and gross hematuria when thin-walled renal varicosities rupture into the collecting system. Because the left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein, patients can also develop a left-sided varicocele.

explanation_incorrect.B: The IMA arises well below the renal vessels and cannot form this compression; the offending anterior vessel is the SMA.
explanation_incorrect.C: This describes SMA syndrome, which produces intermittent postprandial obstruction rather than hematuria and a varicocele.
explanation_incorrect.D: The right renal vein lies near the IVC rather than the SMA, and the nutcracker specifically involves the left renal vein.
explanation_incorrect.E: The compressed structure is the thin-walled left renal vein, not the renal artery; venous congestion explains both the hematuria and the varicocele.

educationalObjective: Nutcracker syndrome is SMA-and-aorta compression of the left renal vein causing flank pain, hematuria, and a left varicocele.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Abdominal aorta, watershed areas, and compression syndromes
vignette: A 19-year-old woman has had 3 weeks of intermittent epigastric fullness and pain shortly after meals, with occasional bilious vomiting. She lost 18 kg after gastric bypass surgery 4 months ago. An upper GI series shows distention of the stomach and proximal duodenum with an abrupt narrowing where the third portion of the duodenum crosses the midline. She has no history of abdominal adhesions.
question: Which of the following best explains this patient's obstruction?

options.text: Compression of the left renal vein between the SMA and aorta.
Compression of the third portion of the duodenum between the celiac trunk and the aorta.
Midgut volvulus around the SMA axis with secondary duodenal obstruction.
Compression of the transverse (third) portion of the duodenum between the SMA and the aorta due to diminished mesenteric fat.
Acute SMA thrombosis with ischemic stricture of the distal duodenum.

explanation_correct: SMA syndrome is intermittent intestinal obstruction, chiefly postprandial pain, caused when the SMA and aorta compress the transverse (third) portion of the duodenum. The mesenteric fat pad normally holds the SMA away from the aorta; it is lost in states such as rapid weight loss, low body weight, malnutrition, and gastric bypass surgery. This is distinct from nutcracker syndrome, in which the same vessels compress the left renal vein.

explanation_incorrect.A: That is nutcracker syndrome; it causes flank pain, gross hematuria, and left varicocele, not postprandial duodenal obstruction.
explanation_incorrect.B: The celiac trunk arises above the duodenum and does not form the aortomesenteric angle; the compressing anterior vessel is the SMA.
explanation_incorrect.C: Midgut volvulus is a rotational abnormality that classically affects infants with bilious vomiting, not an intermittent obstruction linked to loss of mesenteric fat after weight loss.
explanation_incorrect.E: SMA thrombosis produces acute severe ischemic abdominal pain, not chronic intermittent postprandial obstruction with a widely patent proximal duodenum.

educationalObjective: SMA syndrome is postprandial duodenal obstruction from SMA-and-aorta compression of the third duodenum in patients with diminished mesenteric fat.
